mcqs.question: A spinlock is generally a good choice when:
options: The expected wait time is shorter than the cost of a context switch
The critical section might block on a network call
The lock is expected to be held for a long, unpredictable duration
The system only has a single CPU core
mcqs.explanation: Spinlocks pay off exactly when spinning is cheaper than the alternative: a very short expected wait, shorter than a context switch. Blocking or long/unpredictable hold times favor a blocking mutex instead, and single-core systems are the worst case for spinlocks since the holder can't run while another thread spins.

mcqs.question: A kernel routine holds a lock for roughly 10 CPU instructions before releasing it. Which lock type is the better fit, and why?
options: A blocking mutex, because it always uses less memory
A reentrant lock, because the routine might be called recursively
A spinlock, because the hold time is far shorter than a context switch would cost
A reader-writer lock, because multiple readers should be allowed
mcqs.explanation: For a critical section this short, spinning briefly is far cheaper than the two context switches a blocking mutex would cost — this is the textbook spinlock use case inside kernels. Memory footprint isn't the deciding factor here, recursion isn't implied, and there's no reader/writer distinction in this scenario.

mcqs.question: A configuration store is read thousands of times per second and updated roughly once an hour. What's the best locking strategy?
options: A reader-writer lock, letting concurrent reads proceed and serializing only the rare writes
A plain mutex around every read and write, for simplicity
A spinlock, since reads are fast
No locking at all, since reads outnumber writes so heavily
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the read-heavy workload a reader-writer lock is built for: thousands of concurrent readers proceed in parallel, and only the rare write serializes. A plain mutex would needlessly serialize all those reads against each other. Skipping locking entirely still leaves a race against the hourly writer, and a spinlock doesn't address the reader/writer distinction at all.

mcqs.question: A function locks a mutex, then makes a network call to a downstream service before unlocking. Under load, what's the most likely production symptom?
options: Slightly higher memory usage, but no impact on latency
A crash in the downstream service
Request threads pile up waiting for the lock, and overall latency spikes with the slow downstream call
The mutex silently becomes a spinlock
mcqs.explanation: Holding a lock across a blocking call means every other thread wanting that lock waits for the full duration of the network call, so under load, threads queue up behind whichever one is mid-call — a slow downstream dependency turns into an application-wide slowdown. It doesn't crash the downstream service, doesn't just cost memory, and mutex type doesn't change on its own.

mcqs.question: A service's CPU usage looks moderate (around 50%) but latency is high and throughput has plateaued. Thread dumps show dozens of threads BLOCKED on the same monitor. What's the most likely fix?
options: Add more application threads to handle the load
Upgrade to faster CPUs, since the bottleneck is compute
Shrink the critical section or split the single lock into several guarding independent data (lock striping)
Switch the mutex to a spinlock so threads don't sleep
mcqs.explanation: Many threads blocked on the same monitor with only moderate CPU usage is the signature of lock contention, not a compute or thread-count shortage — adding threads would only increase contention. The fix is reducing how much work happens under the lock or splitting it into finer-grained locks. Switching to a spinlock would waste CPU spinning on what's evidently a non-trivial hold time.
